headline: The AI That Writes Code Can't See Its Own Bugs
summary: AI models struggle to find bugs in their own code because they retain the original assumptions. An independent AI reviewer, much like a second human developer, proves essential for catching critical errors.
details: The article highlights an instance where a security hole, allowing root-level shell access via Discord, was almost left open due to a contradictory permission list in the fix. Despite human review, the bug was missed because the initial assumption was that the fix was complete.

A second, independent AI model, however, immediately identified the conflicting "allow" and "deny" lines for the shell command, revealing the flaw. This demonstrated that the original human and AI reviewers were blind to the error due to their initial assumptions.

When an AI reviews its own code, it tends to justify its existing logic rather than critically assess it, acting as a "lawyer for its own code." This self-review fails because the AI carries the same assumptions it had when writing the code.

The solution mirrors human development practices: use a separate AI model for code review. This independent reviewer, free from the original assumptions, can spot issues the authoring AI (and human) overlooked.

Another case involved a blog deployment script where an AI reviewer prevented multiple future posts from going live simultaneously. The initial human focus on "today's post" overlooked the broader implications for the post queue.

These two distinct bugs, one security and one logic, both ran without errors and would have shipped to production without a second pair of eyes. This underscores the value of independent review for catching subtle yet critical flaws.

While a second AI reviewer is valuable, its findings are not absolute. In one instance, a P2 flag for message routing was raised, but human verification confirmed the existing path was correct and the warning was for a very narrow, arguably intended case.

The key takeaway is that the second reviewer acts as a "second opinion," flagging areas for human verification rather than making final decisions. Human developers must still weigh these flags against real code and tests.

The principle is simple: before every code merge, hand the diff to an AI model that didn't write it. This systematic approach ensures consistent, independent review, moving beyond relying on human memory.

headline_marked: [[AI chip maker SambaNova raises $1B]] at $11B valuation, 5 months after last mega round
headline: AI chip maker SambaNova raises $1B at $11B valuation, 5 months after last mega round
summary: SambaNova Systems secures a massive Series F round, boosting its valuation to $11 billion just five months after its previous funding, signaling strong investor confidence in its AI inference technology.
details: AI chip company SambaNova Systems has successfully raised $1 billion in its Series F round, achieving an $11 billion valuation. This initial close was led by General Atlantic, with more investors expected to join soon.

This significant funding comes roughly five months after the Palo Alto-based startup unveiled its SN50 chip and secured a $350 million Series E round in February. The company had previously been in acquisition talks with Intel, reportedly valued at $1.6 billion in December.

CEO Rodrigo Liang remained noncommittal on whether the recent funding rounds solidify SambaNova's independence, noting the company continues to receive acquisition interest. He suggested that current momentum and growth would likely steer the company towards a public offering at some point.

SambaNova's relationship with Intel, a long-time backer and participant in the latest round, has deepened. They announced a multi-year partnership to support AI inference development based on Intel's Xeon chip, co-developing and co-marketing products.

Alongside the new funding, SambaNova announced a major partnership with JPMorgan Chase, which selected the company as an "inference-infrastructure partner." SambaNova's SN40L and SN50 systems will power secure, on-premises AI inference for the bank.

Liang highlighted the JPMorgan win as a crucial signal to the banking industry, encouraging a move away from complete reliance on cloud services. He expects this trend of building private, secure infrastructure for sensitive models to extend beyond banking to other enterprises and governments.

SambaNova positions itself for "premium inference" for the largest models, fitting multi-trillion-parameter models onto a single rack for speed. Its SN40L launched in September 2023, while the next-gen SN50, unveiled in February 2026, is set to ship in H2 2026 with SoftBank as its first partner.

The company targets three customer segments: sovereign clouds, neoclouds, and enterprises building for internal use. Current customers include Saudi Aramco, Intel, and several Japanese firms, in addition to the newly announced JPMorgan Chase.

Proceeds from the Series F round will be used to scale the business and strengthen its supply chain. Liang emphasized securing the supply chain as essential to meet the "incredible wave of demand" and fulfill orders over the next 12 months.

Other notable investors in the round include Seligman Ventures, T. Rowe Price Associates, and Capital Group. Both new and existing investors such as BlackRock, Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), and Vista Equity Partners also participated.
